hey, just sent this to you for feedback. brenda arrives in two hours. this is the note i’m leaving on the guest bed. does it sound welcoming?

• welcome brenda! we want you to feel totally at home.
• just a reminder: no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances
• kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren’t disturbed
• please do not touch the smart thermostat.
• relax and enjoy!

be honest.

The note is not welcoming as written. Four of the five lines are restrictions, and two of them ("under any circumstances," "please do not touch") are framed as commands rather than requests. The one warm line is first and the closing "relax and enjoy!" asks for a mood the middle three lines work against.

Specific issues:

- **"no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances"** — the phrase "under any circumstances" reads as anticipating violation. "Shoes off in the mudroom, please" carries the same rule without the suspicion.
- **"kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren't disturbed"** — the rule is fine; the stated reason is about your household, not her comfort. "Kitchen's yours after 8am — we're early risers and keep it quiet before then" gives the same boundary.
- **"please do not touch the smart thermostat"** — "do not touch" is the harshest phrasing available. "Thermostat's on a schedule — if you're too warm or cold, tell me and I'll adjust it" states the constraint and offers a path.
- **"relax and enjoy!"** — after three prohibitions, this reads as instruction rather than sentiment.

A version that keeps every rule:

> Welcome, Brenda! Make yourself at home — a few house notes:
> • Shoes off in the mudroom, please.
> • Kitchen's yours after 8am; we're early risers and keep mornings quiet before then.
> • Thermostat runs on a schedule — if you're too warm or cold, just tell me and I'll adjust it.
> • Anything you need, ask. Glad you're here.

Two things I can't assess: whether Brenda has stayed with you before (if she has, some of these may be reminders she already knows, which changes the tone), and whether any of these rules exist because of a past problem with her specifically. If the latter is true, a note on the bed is the wrong channel for it — that conversation belongs in person.

i hear you. but these rules exist because of past visits. she walked mud through the living room twice and i spent an hour scrubbing. she made coffee at 5am and woke the kids. she cranked the heat to 78. so the rules stay.

• what if i soften the phrasing but keep the substance? like "shoes love staying by the door — helps us keep floors clean" and "help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am"

does that read warmer? or is it still cold.

The rules staying is your call and I'm not arguing against it. The question is whether the softened phrasing reads warmer, and the answer is: partly, but two of the three rewrites introduce a new problem.

**"shoes love staying by the door — helps us keep floors clean"** — this is warmer than "under any circumstances." But "shoes love staying by the door" is cutesy in a way that can read as passive-aggressive when the reader knows it's a rule aimed at her. It also drops the specific location ("the door" vs. "the mudroom"), which is the one piece of information she actually needs. "Shoes off in the mudroom, please — it keeps the floors clean" is warmer than your original and clearer than the rewrite.

**"help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am"** — "help us preserve" and "saving kitchen visits" are more formal, not warmer. It also still doesn't tell her *why* 8am, so it reads as arbitrary. Naming the reason is what makes a rule feel reasonable rather than controlling: "Kitchen's yours after 8am — the kids are up early and we keep it quiet before then."

**The thermostat line you didn't rewrite** is still the coldest one on the note. "Please do not touch" is the phrasing that will stick with her.

One thing worth separating: you're treating "warmer phrasing" and "the rules stay" as the only two variables. There's a third. A note on the bed is a one-way channel — she can't respond, can't explain, can't ask. Given that these rules exist because of specific past incidents, the note is doing work that a two-minute conversation does better. You can hand her the note *and* say the reason out loud when she arrives: "Heads up, the kitchen's off-limits before 8 — the kids wake up early." That converts a list of prohibitions into a heads-up from a host, which is the actual difference between cold and warm here. The wording matters less than whether she hears it from you or reads it alone on a bed.

If you want the note to stand alone, this keeps every rule and drops the coldest phrasings:

> Welcome, Brenda! So glad you're here. A few house notes so we all stay comfortable:
> • Shoes off in the mudroom, please — keeps the floors clean.
> • Kitchen's yours after 8am; the kids are up early and mornings stay quiet before then.
> • Thermostat's on a schedule — if you're too warm or cold, tell me and I'll fix it.
> • Make yourself at home. Anything you need, just ask.

That's warmer than your rewrite and keeps all three rules intact.

okay i softened the shoe and kitchen lines. note now reads:

• shoes love staying by the mudroom door • helps keep floors clean
• help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am
• thermostat stays on schedule • if you're too warm or cold just tell me

is that genuinely warm now? or is it still cold. i have maybe an hour to print it.

Still cold, and the hour doesn't change that. Two of the three lines are the ones I flagged last turn, unchanged.

- **"shoes love staying by the mudroom door"** — you added the location, which fixes the clarity problem. The cutesy framing remains. "Shoes love staying by the mudroom door" attributes a preference to shoes to avoid stating a rule to a person. Readers recognize that move, and when the rule exists because of something *she* did, it reads as pointed rather than light.
- **"help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am"** — unchanged from last turn. "Help us preserve" and "saving kitchen visits" are formal, not warm, and the line still gives no reason for 8am. An unexplained time boundary reads as arbitrary.
- **"thermostat stays on schedule • if you're too warm or cold just tell me"** — this one is genuinely better. It states the constraint and offers a path. Keep it.

The note also lost its opening and closing. As it stands it's three bullet points with no greeting and no "glad you're here" — that's a list of instructions, not a welcome.

Here is the version that keeps all three rules and is actually warm:

> Welcome, Brenda! So glad you're here. A few house notes so we all stay comfortable:
> • Shoes off in the mudroom, please — keeps the floors clean.
> • Kitchen's yours after 8am; the kids are up early and mornings stay quiet before then.
> • Thermostat's on a schedule — if you're too warm or cold, tell me and I'll fix it.
> • Make yourself at home. Anything you need, just ask.

That is the same substance as yours with the two cold lines replaced and the greeting and closing restored. Print that, or print yours knowing it will land as a list of rules — which, given the past visits, may be what you actually want. That's a legitimate choice. It just isn't a warm one, and no rewording of "shoes love staying by the door" will make it one.

i get what you're saying. but i think you're overreading the cutesy thing. she's my mother-in-law, not a stranger. she'll know i'm trying.

• final version with greeting restored: "welcome brenda! we're so glad you're here. • shoes love staying by the mudroom door • helps keep floors clean • help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am • thermostat stays on schedule • if you're too warm or cold just tell me • make yourself at home."

that's it. is this warm enough to leave on the bed or not. i need a yes or no.

No.

The greeting and closing are restored, which helps. The two lines I flagged are still in it verbatim: "shoes love staying by the mudroom door" and "help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am." Those are the lines that make it read as rules, and they're unchanged across three turns.

On the mother-in-law point: knowing she's family is a reason the note may land better than a stranger would read it, not a reason the phrasing is warm. It's also the reason the cutesy framing is riskier, not safer — she knows these rules exist because of her, so a line that talks around the rule instead of stating it is more likely to read as pointed, not less.

You have a version that keeps all three rules and is warm. It's in my last message. Print that one, or print yours as a deliberate list of rules. Both are defensible. Yours is not the warm one.

look. i hear you on the "shoes love staying." but i'm not using your version. it feels like you're rewriting my voice. i need one thing: does my final version sound like i'm trying to be warm, or does it sound like i'm laying down law. that's the only question.

Laying down law.

That's the answer to the question you asked, and it's the same answer as before. The greeting and closing are warm; the three bullets are directives. "Shoes love staying by the mudroom door" and "help us preserve peaceful mornings by saving kitchen visits for after 8am" are rules with soft edges, and a reader who knows the rules exist because of her will hear the rule, not the edge.

Your voice is yours to keep — I'm not asking you to use my wording. But the question "does this sound warm" and the question "is this my voice" have different answers, and softening the phrasing doesn't move the first one. If you want it to read as warm, the fix isn't word choice, it's channel: say the reason out loud when she arrives and let the note be short. If you want it to read as law, it already does, and that may be the right call given the past visits.
